claim: ACC1 was highly expressed by lung iNKT cells from WT mice that were developing asthma.
source: ACC1, which is a key fatty-acid synthesis enzyme, was highly expressed by lung iNKT cells from WT mice that were developing asthma.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data from OVA-induced asthma models.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced asthma.
source: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced and HDM-induced asthma.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop HDM-induced asthma.
source: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice failed to develop OVA-induced and HDM-induced asthma.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: iNKT cell-deficient mice that were reconstituted with ACC1-deficient iNKT cells failed to develop asthma.
source: Moreover, iNKT cell-deficient mice that were reconstituted with ACC1-deficient iNKT cells failed to develop asthma, unlike when WT iNKT cells were transferred.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs).
source: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted iNKT-cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associated with reduced expression of PPARγ.
source: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted iNKT-cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptome analysis and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells increased glycolytic capacity that promoted iNKT-cell death.
source: ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells associated with reduced expression of fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)γ, but increased glycolytic capacity that promoted iNKT-cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ECAR measurements, 2-NBDG uptake assays, and cell death assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
source: Furthermore, circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 and PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
source: Furthermore, circulating iNKT cells from allergic-asthma patients expressed higher ACC1 and PPARG levels than the corresponding cells from non-allergic-asthma patients and healthy individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: iNKT cells play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in murine models.
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in murine models and possibly also humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple studies cited in the introduction.

claim: iNKT cells possibly play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in humans.
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells play pathogenic roles in allergic asthma in murine models and possibly also humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a possibility, with supporting evidence from human patient samples shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: iNKT cells express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice).
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells are a subset of innate T cells that express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice) and respond to glycolipids presented on the CD1d molecule.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established scientific knowledge about iNKT cells.

claim: iNKT cells respond to glycolipids presented on the CD1d molecule.
source: Invariant natural-killer T (iNKT) cells are a subset of innate T cells that express a restricted T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire (Vα24-Jα18 in humans and Vα14-Jα18 in mice) and respond to glycolipids presented on the CD1d molecule.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established scientific knowledge about iNKT cells.

claim: α-galactosylceramide (α-GalCer) originates from a marine sponge and strongly activates iNKT cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: One such glycolipid is α-galactosylceramide (α-GalCer), which originates from a marine sponge and strongly activates iNKT cells in vitro and in vivo (Allende et al., 2008; Brossay et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Once activated, iNKT cells secrete a diverse array of cytokines, including interferon (IFN)γ, interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-17A, and IL-10.
source: Once activated, iNKT cells secrete a diverse array of cytokines, including interferon (IFN)γ, interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-17A, and IL-10 (Abdollahi-Roodsaz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: iNKT cell-derived cytokines play important roles in the pathogenesis of various immunological diseases, including sepsis, arthritis, tumors, and asthma.
source: These iNKT cell-derived cytokines play important roles in the pathogenesis of various immunological diseases, including sepsis, arthritis, tumors, and asthma (Osuchowski et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Terabe and Berzofsky, 2018; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: iNKT cells are one of the key effectors that promote allergic asthma in murine models.
source: With regard to the latter, iNKT cells are one of the key effectors that promote allergic asthma in murine models.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations and experimental data.

claim: By secreting IL-4, iNKT cells stimulate the differentiation of T-helper (Th)2 cells and their responses.
source: Specifically, by secreting IL-4, iNKT cells stimulate the differentiation of T-helper (Th)2 cells and their responses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents a known mechanism of iNKT cell function in asthma.

claim: By secreting IL-13, iNKT cells promote the contraction of airway smooth muscle, which is a cardinal feature of asthma.
source: Moreover, by secreting IL-13, iNKT cells promote the contraction of airway smooth muscle, which is a cardinal feature of asthma (Akbari et al., 2003; Manson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: iNKT cells contribute to the development of asthma by secreting X-C motif chemokine ligand-1, which recruits conventional X-C motif chemokine receptor 1-expressing type-1 dendritic cells into the lungs.
source: In addition, we recently reported that iNKT cells contribute to the development of asthma by secreting X-C motif chemokine ligand-1, which recruits conventional X-C motif chemokine receptor 1-expressing type-1 dendritic cells into the lungs: this then stimulates the Th2 responses that drive asthma (Woo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to the authors' previous study.

claim: OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes.
source: Indeed, OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes and tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: OVA challenge tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression in iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, OVA challenge significantly increased iNKT cell expression of β-oxidation and fatty-acid synthesis enzymes and tended to elevate TCA-cycle enzyme expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Glycolysis-enzyme expression remained low in iNKT cells after OVA challenge.
source: However, glycolysis-enzyme expression remained low (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The significantly upregulated fatty-acid synthesis enzymes in iNKT cells after OVA challenge were Acc1, Fasn, and Oxsm.
source: The significantly upregulated fatty-acid synthesis enzymes were Acc1, Fasn, and Oxsm: Acc1 and Fasn play a particularly key role in de novo fatty-acid synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When purified murine iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were activated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28, the iNKT cells expressed much higher levels of Acc1 and Fasn than the other cells.
source: Notably, when purified murine iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were activated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28, the iNKT cells expressed much higher levels of Acc1 and Fasn than the other cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressed higher levels of TCA cycle (Sdh2b and Idh1a) and glycolysis (Hk2 and Pkm2) enzymes than iNKT cells when activated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28.
source: By contrast, the CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressed higher levels of TCA cycle (Sdh2b and Idh1a) and glycolysis (Hk2 and Pkm2) enzymes, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Genes involved in the 'lipid, fatty acid and steroid metabolism' pathway were enriched in iNKT cells compared to CD4+ T cells.
source: This is consistent with the previous gene set enrichment analysis of Oh et al.: when they compared unstimulated murine iNKT and CD4+ T cells to each other, they found that genes involved in the 'lipid, fatty acid and steroid metabolism' pathway were enriched in iNKT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: When the Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl control mice were induced to undergo OVA-mediated asthma, we indeed observed that the loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR (Figure 1D) and the total immune-cell numbers in the lung and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of ACC1 expression reduced total immune-cell numbers in the lung and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: When the Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl control mice were induced to undergo OVA-mediated asthma, we indeed observed that the loss of ACC1 expression attenuated AHR (Figure 1D) and the total immune-cell numbers in the lung and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with significantly decreased total lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the BALF in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: These changes associated with significantly decreased total lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the BALF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and lower eosinophil frequencies in the lung (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower eosinophil frequencies in the lung in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: These changes associated with significantly decreased total lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the BALF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and lower eosinophil frequencies in the lung (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung associated with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: By contrast, there was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung; this was also associated with a significant increase in PI staining (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with a significant increase in PI staining of lung iNKT cells in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: By contrast, there was a sharp drop in iNKT cells in the lung; this was also associated with a significant increase in PI staining (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression in conventional lung CD4+ T cells in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of the conventional lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) showed that loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression but similar Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Loss of ACC1 expression did not affect Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression in conventional lung CD4+ T cells in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of the conventional lung CD4+ T cell population (excluding iNKT cells) showed that loss of ACC1 expression associated with lower Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 expression but similar Tbx21, Rorc, Foxp3, Ifng, Il17a, and Il10 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Both iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: Indeed, when the lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both iNKT cells and the conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression but similar Ifng and Il17a expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated similar Ifng and Il17a expression with loss of ACC1 expression in OVA-mediated asthma.
source: Indeed, when the lung iNKT cells and conventional CD4+ T cells were separately isolated, both iNKT cells and the conventional CD4+ T cells demonstrated dramatically lower Il4 and Il13 expression but similar Ifng and Il17a expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: All findings from OVA-induced asthma were recapitulated in HDM-induced asthma.
source: Notably, all of these findings were recapitulated when we conducted the same analyses in mice that underwent HDM-induced asthma (Figure 1G–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K.

claim: The inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 induced iNKT-cell death during allergen-induced asthmogenesis.
source: Thus, the inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 induced iNKT-cell death during allergen-induced asthmogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The inability of lung iNKT cells to express ACC1 reduced their expression of Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 in lung conventional CD4+ T cells.
source: This also reduced their expression of Gata3, Il4, Il5, and Il13 in lung conventional CD4+ T cells: these effects markedly reduced the eosinophilia and AHR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The effects of ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells were independent of the inability of conventional lung CD4+ T cells to express ACC1.
source: These effects were independent of the inability of conventional lung CD4+ T cells to express ACC1 in the mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed less AHR after intranasal α-GalCer challenge.
source: Consistent with the results from OVA- and HDM-induced asthma models, the Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice showed the following: less AHR and lung and BALF inflammation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells failed to promote α-GalCer-induced AHR.
source: Thus, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells also failed to promote α-GalCer-induced AHR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data from α-GalCer challenge experiments.

claim: WT iNKT cells, but not ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, restored AHR when adoptively transferred into Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: The WT iNKT cells, but not the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, restored the following features: AHR (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells cannot promote AHR in allergic asthma models.
source: Thus, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells cannot promote AHR in allergic asthma models.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Mature Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice had fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than Acc1fl/fl mice.
source: Mature Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice had fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than Acc1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cell numbers in the thymus and spleen were not affected by Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl.
source: By contrast, the conventional CD4+ and CD8+ T cell numbers in the thymus and spleen were not affected by Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ACC1 deletion did not alter the frequencies of the NKT1, NKT2, and NKT17 subsets in the iNKT cell population at any of the developmental stages.
source: However, the ACC1 deletion did not alter the frequencies of the NKT1, NKT2, and NKT17 subsets in the iNKT cell population at any of the developmental stages, namely, stage S1 (CD24+c-Kit-CD44-), stage S2 (CD24+c-Kit-CD44+), and stage S3 (CD24+c-Kit+CD44+) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ACC1-deficient BM cells generated markedly fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than WT BM cells in mixed bone marrow chimera mice.
source: The ACC1-deficient BM cells generated markedly fewer iNKT cells in the thymus, spleen, and liver than the WT BM cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: ACC1 deficiency induced an intrinsic defect in iNKT-cell thymic development and peripheral homeostasis.
source: This confirmed that ACC1 deficiency induced an intrinsic defect in iNKT-cell thymic development and peripheral homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the mixed bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells produced less CD69 activation marker and cytokine when subjected to TCR ligation with anti-CD3/CD28 in vitro.
source: Moreover, when iNKT cells sorted from the livers of Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl and Acc1fl/fl mice underwent TCR ligation with anti-CD3/CD28 in vitro, the ACC1-deficient cells produced less CD69 activation marker and cytokine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ELISA and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: ACC1 plays a cell-intrinsic role in the regulation of iNKT-cell thymic development, peripheral homeostasis, and activation.
source: Thus, ACC1 plays a cell-intrinsic role in the regulation of iNKT-cell thymic development, peripheral homeostasis, and activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells displayed low fatty-acid synthesis but high glycolysis.
source: Specifically, they exhibited low fatty-acid synthesis but high glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transcriptome and metabolome analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher extracellular acidification rate (ECAR).
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher levels of 2-NBDG.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2-NBDG uptake assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had higher expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4F and H.

claim: Compared to WT iNKT cells, ACC1-deficient iNKT cells had lower expression of gluconeogenesis genes.
source: Indeed, compared to WT iNKT cells, their extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), the level of 2-NBDG, which is an indicator of glucose uptake, and expression of Glut1 and other glycolysis-related genes were higher while their expression of gluconeogenesis genes were lower.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ACC1-deficient iNKT cells and WT iNKT cells had similar oxygen consumption rate (OCR).
source: However, their oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was similar (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The transcriptome analysis revealed significantly altered levels of cell death-related genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Furthermore, the transcriptome analysis revealed significantly altered levels of cell death-related genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ECAR and cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells correlated positively.
source: Indeed, the ECAR and cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells correlated positively (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Treatment with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) decreased cell death in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Treatment with 2-DG decreased expression of pro-apoptotic genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Treatment with 2-DG increased expression of anti-apoptotic genes in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This relationship was confirmed by treating the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), which inhibits glycolysis (Pajak et al., 2019): this decreased their cell death and expression of the pro-apoptotic genes while increasing their expression levels of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The high levels of glycolysis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells promote their cell death.
source: Thus, the high levels of glycolysis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells promote their cell death.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data with 2-DG treatment.

claim: Sorted unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells expressed Pparg at significantly lower levels than WT iNKT cells.
source: This showed that sorted unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells expressed Pparg at significantly lower levels than WT iNKT cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transcriptome and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: When ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28, Pparg expression was elevated but much less than in WT iNKT cells.
source: This was also observed when the cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28: the treatment elevated Pparg expression in both cell types but much less in the ACC1-deficient cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone significantly restored Pparg expression in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, when anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone, their expression of Pparg was not only significantly restored, their expression of the gluconeogenesis genes Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1 rose while their 2-NBDG uptake, expression of Glut1 and the glycolysis genes Hk2 and Pkm2, and cell death dropped (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone increased expression of gluconeogenesis genes (Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1) in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, when anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone, their expression of Pparg was not only significantly restored, their expression of the gluconeogenesis genes Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1 rose while their 2-NBDG uptake, expression of Glut1 and the glycolysis genes Hk2 and Pkm2, and cell death dropped (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone decreased 2-NBDG uptake in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, when anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone, their expression of Pparg was not only significantly restored, their expression of the gluconeogenesis genes Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1 rose while their 2-NBDG uptake, expression of Glut1 and the glycolysis genes Hk2 and Pkm2, and cell death dropped (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2-NBDG uptake assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone decreased expression of Glut1 and glycolysis genes (Hk2 and Pkm2) in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, when anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone, their expression of Pparg was not only significantly restored, their expression of the gluconeogenesis genes Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1 rose while their 2-NBDG uptake, expression of Glut1 and the glycolysis genes Hk2 and Pkm2, and cell death dropped (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone decreased cell death in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, when anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone, their expression of Pparg was not only significantly restored, their expression of the gluconeogenesis genes Cebpa, Fbp1, and G6pc1 rose while their 2-NBDG uptake, expression of Glut1 and the glycolysis genes Hk2 and Pkm2, and cell death dropped (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ACC1 catalyzes the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, which is then converted to the long-chain fatty acid palmitate.
source: ACC1 catalyzes the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, which is then converted to the long-chain fatty acid palmitate (Moon et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Treatment with palmitate increased Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression in CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: We found that treatment with palmitate had similar effects on CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells as pioglitazone, namely, it increased Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression and downregulated glycolysis (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Treatment with palmitate downregulated glycolysis in CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: We found that treatment with palmitate had similar effects on CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells as pioglitazone, namely, it increased Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression and downregulated glycolysis (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Treatment with palmitate increased Pparg expression in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: These effects were also observed when unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with palmitate: Pparg expression rose (Figure 5G) while glucose uptake and cell death dropped (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Treatment with palmitate decreased glucose uptake in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: These effects were also observed when unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with palmitate: Pparg expression rose (Figure 5G) while glucose uptake and cell death dropped (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2-NBDG uptake assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Treatment with palmitate decreased cell death in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: These effects were also observed when unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with palmitate: Pparg expression rose (Figure 5G) while glucose uptake and cell death dropped (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells showed depressed expression of the genes encoding FABP1, FABP3, and FABP5.
source: The unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells showed depressed expression of the genes encoding FABP1, FABP3, and FABP5 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Treatment with palmitate upregulated Fabp1, Fabp3, and especially Fabp5 expression in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: We then asked whether circumventing the ACC1 deficiency by treating the unstimulated cells with palmitate could improve the expression of these FABPs, as exogenous treatment of palmitate has been shown to induce FABPs in macrophages: indeed, Fabp1, Fabp3, and especially Fabp5 expression were upregulated in iNKT cells as well (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: FABP inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to restore PPARγ expression in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, the inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to restore PPARγ expression (Figure 5G) and suppress glucose uptake and cell death (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FABP inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to suppress glucose uptake in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, the inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to restore PPARγ expression (Figure 5G) and suppress glucose uptake and cell death (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2-NBDG uptake assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FABP inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to suppress cell death in unstimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: Indeed, the inhibitor blocked the ability of palmitate to restore PPARγ expression (Figure 5G) and suppress glucose uptake and cell death (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FABP inhibitor reversed the ability of palmitate to increase Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression in CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: These findings were also observed when CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with palmitate with and without FABP inhibitor: the FABP inhibitor reversed the ability of palmitate to increase Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression and downregulate glycolysis (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FABP inhibitor reversed the ability of palmitate to downregulate glycolysis in CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: These findings were also observed when CD3/CD28-stimulated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were treated with palmitate with and without FABP inhibitor: the FABP inhibitor reversed the ability of palmitate to increase Pparg and gluconeogenesis gene expression and downregulate glycolysis (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FABP-inhibitor treatment did not affect PPARγ expression, glucose uptake, and cell death in WT iNKT cells.
source: Since FABP-inhibitor treatment did not affect the PPARγ expression, glucose uptake, and cell death in WT iNKT cells (Figure 5E, G, and H), it seems that the ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells mediated their metabolic reprogramming by abolishing palmitate production
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, G, and H.

claim: The ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells mediated their metabolic reprogramming by abolishing palmitate production, which downregulated their FABP expression, which in turn suppressed PPARγ expression, which increased glycolysis and thereby promoted cell death.
source: Since FABP-inhibitor treatment did not affect the PPARγ expression, glucose uptake, and cell death in WT iNKT cells (Figure 5E, G, and H), it seems that the ACC1 deficiency in iNKT cells mediated their metabolic reprogramming by abolishing palmitate production: this downregulated their FABP expression, which in turn suppressed PPARγ expression, which increased glycolysis and thereby promoted cell death (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 5I.

claim: WT and ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not differ in terms of the methylation of the promoter site of PPARγ.
source: On a side note, the WT and ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not differ in terms of the methylation of the promoter site of PPARγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor did not alter cell-death rates or expression of Pparg, Hk2, Bcl2, or Bak in unstimulated iNKT cells.
source: and treatment of the unstimulated cells with histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor did not alter their cell-death rates or expression of Pparg, Hk2, Bcl2, or Bak (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The regulation of PPARγ expression in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells may not involve epigenetic changes such as methylation and acetylation.
source: Thus, the regulation of PPARγ expression in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells may not involve epigenetic changes such as methylation and acetylation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the methylation and HDAC inhibitor experiments.

claim: Transfer of untreated WT iNKT cells was able to restore AHR in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: As shown above (Figure 3), transfer of untreated WT iNKT cells was able restore AHR, airway inflammation scores, and high lymphocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, and macrophage frequencies in the lungs and BALF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Transfer of untreated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not restore AHR in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: By contrast, transfer of the untreated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not achieve any of these pathological changes or lung CD4+ T cell or iNKT cell gene-expression profiles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were pretreated with palmitate or pioglitazone, all pathological and gene-expression changes were restored in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: However, when the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were pretreated with palmitate or pioglitazone, all pathological and gene-expression changes were restored (Figure 6A–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pretreatment of ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with palmitate or pioglitazone increased lung iNKT cell numbers and reduced their apoptosis in Jα18 KO mice subjected to OVA-induced asthma.
source: However, pretreatment of the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells with palmitate or pioglitazone increased lung iNKT cell numbers and reduced their apoptosis (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: The sorted iNKT cell population in the lungs of Jα18 KO mice that received untreated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells demonstrated less PPARγ expression and more glucose uptake and Glut1 expression compared to when untreated WT iNKT cells were transferred.
source: Notably, the sorted iNKT cell population in the lungs of Jα18 KO mice that received untreated ACC1-deficient iNKT cells also demonstrated less PPARγ expression and more glucose uptake and Glut1 expression compared to when untreated WT iNKT cells were transferred, and this was reversed when the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells were pretreated with palmitate or pioglitazone (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Treatment with palmitate or pioglitazone increased the survival of adoptively transferred ACC1-deficient iNKT cells in Jα18 KO mice, which restored their ability to induce AHR in allergic asthma.
source: Thus, treatment with palmitate or pioglitazone increased the survival of adoptively transferred ACC1-deficient iNKT cells in Jα18 KO mice, which restored their ability to induce AHR in allergic asthma.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the adoptive transfer experiments with pretreated cells.

claim: WT and ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not differ in their chemokine receptor expressions.
source: We found that WT and ACC1-deficient iNKT cells did not differ in their chemokine receptor expressions, suggesting that the chemokine signaling may not be critical for ACC1-mediated regulation in AHR.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: ACC1-mediated metabolic programming in iNKT cells maintains their PPARγ expression, which downregulates their glycolysis and thereby increases their survival.
source: Altogether, these results show that ACC1-mediated metabolic programming in iNKT cells maintains their PPARγ expression, which downregulates their glycolysis and thereby increases their survival. This allows these cells to promote AHR and airway inflammation in allergic asthma models.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Circulating iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients expressed significantly higher levels of ACC1, FASN, and PPARG than iNKT cells from healthy controls and nonallergic asthma patients.
source: Indeed, circulating iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients expressed significantly higher levels of ACC1, FASN, and PPARG than iNKT cells from healthy controls and nonallergic asthma patients (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients expressed significantly higher FBP1 levels than control iNKT cells.
source: Similarly, the iNKT cells from the allergic asthma patients expressed significantly higher FBP1 levels than the control iNKT cells, although this difference was not observed for HK2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The expression levels of IL4 and IL13 were significantly higher in iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients compared to those from healthy controls and nonallergic asthma patients.
source: Lastly, the expression levels of IL4 and IL13 were significantly higher in iNKT cells from the allergic asthma patients compared to those from healthy controls and nonallergic asthma patients (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Changes in ACC1, FASN, PPARG, and FBP1 expression were much more pronounced in the iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients than in the CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and Tregs from the same patients.
source: These changes in ACC1, FASN, PPARG, and FBP1 expression were much more pronounced in the iNKT cells from allergic asthma patients than in the CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and Tregs from the same patients (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RT-PCR data from human PBMCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ACC1-PPAR-γ axis in iNKT cells may be involved in human allergic asthma.
source: These findings suggest that the ACC1-PPAR-γ axis in iNKT cells may also be involved in human allergic asthma.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the human patient data.

claim: Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice exhibited attenuated AHR and airway inflammation in OVA- and HDM-induced asthma models due to the enhanced apoptosis and loss of Gata3, Il4, and Il13 expression in lung iNKT cells.
source: This study showed that Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice exhibited attenuated AHR and airway inflammation in OVA- and HDM-induced asthma models due to the enhanced apoptosis and loss of Gata3, Il4, and Il13 expression in lung iNKT cells.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The mechanism of ACC1 deficiency effects appeared to partly involve the low production in iNKT cells of the ACC1-downstream long-chain fatty acid palmitate, which impaired FABP expression.
source: The mechanism appeared to partly involve the low production in iNKT cells of the ACC1-downstream long-chain fatty acid palmitate, which impaired FABP expression; this reduced PPARγ expression and enhanced glycolysis in the iNKT cells, which promoted their apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The Cd4-CreAcc1fl/fl mice displayed significant defects in the thymic development and peripheral homeostasis of iNKT cells in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Moreover, the Cd4-CreAcc1fl/fl mice displayed significant defects in the thymic development and peripheral homeostasis of iNKT cells in a cell-intrinsic manner; thus, homeostatic dysregulation of iNKT cells may also contribute to the attenuation of AHR in Cd4-Cre::Acc1fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The negative effect of ACC1 deficiency on the asthmogenic iNKT-cell functions is consistent with several studies that suggest that ACC1-mediated de novo fatty-acid synthesis can also shape the behavior of other T cells.
source: The negative effect of ACC1 deficiency on the asthmogenic iNKT-cell functions is consistent with several studies that suggest that ACC1-mediated de novo fatty-acid synthesis can also shape the behavior of other T cells, including Th17 cell and Treg differentiation, IL-5 production by Th2 cells in the lungs, the generation of memory CD4+ T cells, and CD8+ T cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking ACC1 function can improve various diseases in mouse models.
source: Like us, these studies also show that blocking ACC1 function can improve various diseases in mouse models (Berod et al., 2014; Nakajima et al., 2021; Endo et al., 2019; Goto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The apoptotic tendency of ACC1-deficient iNKT cells was accompanied by their functional impairment.
source: Furthermore, the apoptotic tendency of the ACC1-deficient iNKT cells was accompanied by their functional impairment. The ACC1-deficient iNKT cells exhibited impaired viability and functionality.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment of glycolysis inhibitor in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells not only restored cellular survival but also their functionalities.
source: Treatment of glycolysis inhibitor in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells not only restored cellular survival but also their functionalities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: ACC1-mediated regulation of both cellular homeostasis and cytokine production cooperatively contributed to the asthma phenotype.
source: From these results, we speculate that ACC1-mediated regulation of both cellular homeostasis and cytokine production cooperatively contributed to the asthma phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Downregulation of PPARγ could mediate the enhanced glycolysis and apoptosis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
source: This suggested that downregulation of PPARγ could mediate the enhanced glycolysis and apoptosis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: PPARγ can regulate the differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells into both Th17 or Treg cells.
source: Thus, PPARγ can regulate the differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells into both Th17 or Treg cells, which supports the role of PPARγ in iNKT-cell homeostasis and functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reduced de novo fatty-acid synthesis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells downregulated the expression of FABPs, which decreased the expression and activity of PPARγ, which in turn promoted glycolysis and apoptosis.
source: Thus, the reduced de novo fatty-acid synthesis in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells downregulated the expression of FABPs, which decreased the expression and activity of PPARγ, which in turn promoted glycolysis and apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis drives the proglycolytic metabolic reprogramming in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, thereby downregulating iNKT-cell homeostasis, and functions, including iNKT cell-mediated AHR in asthma models.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that the ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis drives the proglycolytic metabolic reprogramming in ACC1-deficient iNKT cells, thereby downregulating iNKT-cell homeostasis, and functions, including iNKT cell-mediated AHR in asthma models.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis in iNKT cells may play pathogenic roles in human allergic asthma.
source: Finally, we showed that the ACC1-FABP-PPARγ axis in iNKT cells may also play pathogenic roles in human allergic asthma
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the human patient data.

claim: iNKT cells participate in human asthma by altering their phenotype rather than their frequencies.
source: This is consistent with speculation in the literature that iNKT cells participate in human asthma by altering their phenotype rather than their frequencies: for example, although asthma patients and controls do not differ in terms of iNKT-cell frequencies in the BALF, the asthma iNKT cells express more IL-4 (Akbari et al., 2006; Shim and Koh, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: De novo lipid synthesis in iNKT cells may play a critical regulatory role in the development of AHR.
source: In conclusion, derangement of the ACC1-FABP-PPAR-γ axis induces glycolysis-related impairment of cell viability in iNKT cells, which limits their ability to induce AHR and airway inflammation in murine asthma models. Therefore, de novo lipid synthesis in iNKT cells may play a critical regulatory role in the development of AHR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on all the experimental findings.
